title: Find employees who earn more than their department's average.
shortTitle: Find employees who earn more than their department's average

s1_definition.profdef: You precompute each department's average salary, then stream the employees and keep those whose salary exceeds the average of their own department. It is a two-pass correlated filter against a per-group aggregate.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya calculates the average pay in each department, then keeps the employees who earn more than their department's average.
s1_definition.oneliner: Precompute per-department averages, then `filter(e -> salary > avg[dept])`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You precompute each department's average salary, then stream the employees and keep those whose salary exceeds the average of their own department. It is a two-pass correlated filter against a per-group aggregate.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya calculates the average pay in each department, then keeps the employees who earn more than their department's average.

**One line to remember:** Precompute per-department averages, then `filter(e -> salary > avg[dept])`.

sections.s2_technical:
First build `Map<String, Double> avgByDept = staff.stream().collect(groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, averagingDouble(Employee::getSalaryAsDouble)))`. Then `staff.stream().filter(e -> e.getSalaryAsDouble() > avgByDept.get(e.getDepartment())).toList()` retains employees above their department's average.

Two passes are required because the comparison depends on an aggregate over the whole department, which cannot be known mid-stream. The map lookup is O(1), making the filter pass linear. This is the correlated-subquery pattern expressed with streams.

The senior nuance is that you cannot fold this into one naive stream — the per-group average must exist before any employee can be judged, so precomputing the map is the clean approach. I guard null departments so the lookup does not fail, and I return the employees themselves or their names depending on the consumer. For exact figures I would average in BigDecimal. Recognising the two-pass structure is the essential insight.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A talent-review at the National Bank of India identifies employees earning above their department average as candidates for stretch assignments.

This is exactly what precompute-averages then correlated-filter does — it keeps the above-average earners per department.

The code defines an `TalentReviewService.aboveOwnDeptAverage method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh IT 1,000,000, Amit IT 600,000, Priya Sales 950,000, Neha Sales 500,000.

Step 1: Pass one computes IT average 800,000 and Sales average 725,000.

Step 2: Pass two keeps employees above their own department average.

Step 3: Rajesh beats IT's 800,000 and Priya beats Sales' 725,000, so both are kept.

Step 4: Amit and Neha are below and dropped.

```
INFO: Above own-dept average: [Rajesh, Priya]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  pass 1: groupingBy(dept, averagingDouble) → {IT=800k, Sales=725k}
  pass 2:
  [Rajesh/IT/1M, Amit/IT/600k, Priya/Sales/950k, Neha/Sales/500k]
    │ filter(salary > avgByDept.get(dept))
    ▼
  [Rajesh, Priya]
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — correlated filter (two-pass) ═══

  ┌─ aggregate then compare ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ pass 1: groupingBy(dept, averagingDouble) → avg per dept    │
  │ pass 2: filter(salary > avgByDept.get(dept))               │
  │ two passes: per-group aggregate must exist before compare   │
  │ map.get O(1) → linear filter pass                          │
  │ SQL analogue: correlated subquery on dept average           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │         TalentReviewService   │
  │  + aboveOwnDeptAverage(List)    │ avg map → correlated filter
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. groupingBy(dept, averagingDouble) → avgByDept
  2. filter(salary > avgByDept.get(dept)).map(name)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To find employees earning more than their department's average I use a two-pass approach. The first pass groups by department and averages the salaries to build a map from department to its average. The second pass streams the employees again and keeps each one whose salary exceeds the average of their own department, looked up from that map. At the National Bank of India this backs a talent review that surfaces above-average earners as candidates for stretch assignments.

The reason it must be two passes is that the comparison value — the department average — is itself an aggregate over the entire department, so it cannot be known while I am still iterating the employees for the first time. Precomputing the averages into a map makes the second pass a clean linear filter, since each lookup is constant time.

The senior point I stress is recognising this as the stream equivalent of a SQL correlated subquery, where each row is compared against an aggregate of its own group. That recognition tells me immediately that a single naive stream will not work and that I need to materialise the per-group averages first. I guard null departments so the lookup never fails, and for an authoritative figure I compute the averages in BigDecimal rather than double.
